summary: An informational memo describing KOI8-U, a character encoding for Ukrainian text that was widely used in the Ukrainian Internet community. It is an extension of the Russian KOI8 encoding.

eli5.summary: Computers store letters as numbers. This memo is the number-to-letter chart for Ukrainian letters that many people used.

questions: how does koi8-u support ukrainian letters
subtitle: A character encoding that allows computers to display Ukrainian text correctly.

tldr.problem: Ukraine's Internet community needed a standard way to encode Ukrainian letters in email and web pages, but existing encodings were designed for Russian or lacked Ukrainian-specific letters.
tldr.mechanism: KOI8-U extends the Russian KOI8-R encoding with four additional Ukrainian letters (ie, i, yi, and ghe with upturn) in specific character positions, while keeping full compatibility with KOI8-R for all Russian letters.
tldr.outcome: KOI8-U became the de-facto standard for Ukrainian Internet communication in the 1990s and 2000s, supported by many email clients, web browsers, and operating systems across Ukraine.

facts.label: Ukrainian-specific letters
facts.value: 4 pairs (8 total with upper and lower case)

today: RFC 2319 remains an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. KOI8-U is now primarily of historical interest, as UTF-8 has become the dominant encoding for international text on the Internet and in most modern systems. However, KOI8-U remains supported in many legacy systems, email archives, and specialized applications that maintain Ukrainian text from the 1990s and 2000s.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
KOI8-U (KOI8 Ukrainian) is a character encoding created to allow computers to display Ukrainian text correctly. Character encoding is a system that assigns a number to each letter so computers can store and transmit letters as numbers. KOI8-U was adopted by the Ukrainian Internet community in 1992, refined in 1995, and became widely supported in email, web browsers, fonts, and operating system locales.

The name KOI8 comes from "Kodirovka Obmena Informatsiei 8 bit" (Information Exchange Coding, 8-bit) in Russian. Ukrainian Internet users adopted this family of encodings because it was lightweight and well-established in the former Soviet space.
sections.eli5: Ukrainian people on the Internet needed a way to write Ukrainian letters in email and websites. KOI8-U is the numbering system they used to do this.

sections.title: Relationship to KOI8-R
sections.content:
KOI8-U is based on KOI8-R, the Russian character encoding defined in RFC 1489. The lower 128 characters (0-127) are identical to ASCII, preserving compatibility with plain English text and basic computer systems. The upper 128 characters (128-255) contain Cyrillic letters and box-drawing symbols for making text boxes and tables in terminals.

KOI8-U includes all 33 Russian letters found in KOI8-R, plus four additional Ukrainian letters that do not exist in Russian: ie (positions 164/180), i (positions 166/182), yi (positions 167/183), and ghe with upturn (positions 173/189). Each Ukrainian letter has both lowercase and uppercase versions. The remaining box-drawing symbols match those in KOI8-R, ensuring visual compatibility.
sections.eli5: KOI8-U starts with all the Russian KOI8 letters, then adds four extra letters that only Ukrainian uses. Both Russian and Ukrainian text can be displayed with the same encoding.

sections.title: Character Encoding Specification
sections.content:
KOI8-U assigns 256 possible values (0-255) to characters. The entire upper half (128-255) is documented in the RFC using Unicode references so that the characters can be precisely identified. For example, position 164 (hex A4) maps to Unicode U+0454, the Cyrillic small letter Ukrainian ie.

The RFC provides a complete table of all 256 mappings, organized by decimal position, hexadecimal code, Unicode equivalent, and character name. This allows any programmer or system to correctly implement KOI8-U without ambiguity. Box-drawing characters are included for terminal display, allowing Ukrainian text to be framed with lines in command-line interfaces. The encoding also defines special symbols like the degree sign, copyright symbol, and mathematical operators.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives a complete list showing which number maps to which letter, so every computer can use KOI8-U the same way.

sections.title: Deployment and Support
sections.content:
By the time this RFC was published in April 1998, KOI8-U was already a de-facto standard supported across the Ukrainian Internet community. The encoding was incorporated into many operating systems' locale support, email clients, and web browsers. Font files were created with Ukrainian letters mapped to KOI8-U positions. MIME (the email standard) recognized koi8-u as an official charset name, allowing email systems to correctly label and interpret Ukrainian text.

The Ukrainian Internet Service Provider community had formally adopted the specification at a 1992 conference in Slavsk, and many contributing individuals and organizations worked to refine and promote it. The RFC documents this consensus by listing the KOI8-U Working Group members and acknowledging the contributors who developed and tested the encoding across diverse systems.
sections.eli5: By 1998, Ukrainian email and web programs already used KOI8-U. This RFC officially documented it so everyone would do it the same way.

sections.title: MIME Registration and Standards
sections.content:
This RFC serves as an Informational document, which means it documents existing practice rather than defining a new standard to be implemented. However, it is the authoritative reference for KOI8-U. The document allows the Internet community to register koi8-u as an official MIME charset, which enables email and web systems to label Ukrainian-encoded messages correctly.

The standards are based on related RFCs: RFC 1489 for KOI8-R, RFC 1345 for character mnemonics, and references to ISO-IR-111 (the International Register assignment for Ukrainian characters) and ISO 10646 (the international standard that became Unicode). This grounding in international standards ensures that KOI8-U correctly maps Ukrainian letters to their Unicode equivalents.
sections.eli5: This RFC makes KOI8-U official so that email systems know to use it for Ukrainian text.
